lec05kp10-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp10-u01-p9-title.text: Why the region count is a sum of binomials, the mean squared error and the checkpoint code

lec05kp10-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp10-u01-p9-bridge.text: Three parallel lines give only four bands, and exercise 1 keeps epoch 2. Why is the region-count formula a sum of binomial coefficients?

lec05kp10-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp10-u01-p9-c1.text: **Recursion**: adding the $K$-th hyperplane in general position cuts some regions in two; the new parts correspond to the lower-dimensional regions the other $K-1$ hyperplanes form on it, so $R(K,d)=R(K-1,d)+R(K-1,d-1)$ with $R(0,d)=R(K,0)=1$. Pascal's relation gives $R(K,d)=\sum_{m=0}^{d}\binom Km$; this counts only the partition of space, not whether the output layer can label any region correctly.

lec05kp10-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp10-u01-p9-c2.text: **Mean squared error**: the loss of each checkpoint can be computed as the mean squared error $L=\dfrac1N\sum_{n=1}^{N}(y_n-\hat y_n)^2$, with $y_n$ the target and $\hat y_n$ the output; the training loss uses the training set and the validation loss the validation set.

lec05kp10-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp10-u01-p9-c3.text: **Program**: `best = min(range(len(val)), key=val.__getitem__) + 1` gives epoch 3 for `[0.55,0.35,0.25,0.28,0.40]`; it picks an existing checkpoint only.

steps.label: Network size and early stopping
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp10 with view-from-text-v2: the pages were planned first (which figure covers which lecture sections) and each page is mainly one native infographic, with the terms defined inside the same figure. 6 main pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). The checkpoint losses and the points on the first page are hand-made teaching illustrations, not experiments; the region bounds and exercise numbers were checked by program or by hand; the source's sine demo was not re-run. English version.

steps.label: Generalization and overfitting
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP10, following the cost function chosen in KP09. The question: with a very high training score, will new data also be right? The points are a noisy teaching illustration, not a network training result. The smooth green curve is the main pattern; the red zigzag passes through every point, so its training error is smallest, but it memorized the noise as well. Three cards on the right: generalization is still predicting new data correctly that did not take part in training; underfitting is failing even to express the main pattern, so training and new data can both be poor; overfitting is fitting accidental details of the training data and hurting predictions on new data. Note that a larger model alone does not imply overfitting; validation results decide. The next page asks how many adjustable numbers a network really has.

steps.label: Free parameters
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page asked whether a high training score means learning. This page first counts the size of the network. Take a 2-3-1 fully connected network: 2 inputs, 3 hidden units, 1 output. Each hidden unit has 2 weights plus 1 bias, 3 numbers, so three units give 2 plus 1 times 3, which is 9; the output unit has 3 weights plus 1 bias, 3 plus 1 times 1, which is 4; the total is 9 plus 4, which is 13. A free parameter is a number that can be changed independently in training, weights and biases both count, so it is not just three hidden units. Count the adjustable numbers first, then ask whether the model is too large or too small. The next page asks when training should stop.

steps.label: Early stopping
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page counted 13 free parameters. This page asks how far to train. The chart shows the losses of five checkpoints, hand-made teaching numbers, not an experiment. Blue is the training loss, falling to 0.10 at epoch 5; orange is the validation loss, lowest at epoch 3 with 0.25, then rising to 0.28 at epoch 4 and 0.40 at epoch 5, 0.15 above the minimum. The validation set is data that does not update weights and is used to choose the model or checkpoint. With the architecture fixed, further training chases details of the training set and makes validation worse; that is overtraining. Stopping by validation performance and restoring the best checkpoint is early stopping: keep epoch 3. The next page asks what roles the validation, training and test data each play.

steps.label: Three data roles
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page used the validation loss to choose epoch 3. This page separates the three kinds of data. The training set updates the weights and learns the pattern in the data, but its score cannot prove that new data are also right. The validation set chooses the size, penalty strength and stopping point, but does not update weights directly. The test set is used for the final evaluation only after the model is chosen; looking at it repeatedly to pick models makes it no longer independent, and repeated individuals or time information must not leak. Small samples are coarse: one error in ten is 1 over 10, which is 0.1, and two errors give 0.2. The next page asks whether network size can be estimated by counting geometric regions.

steps.label: Geometric capacity and XOR
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page separated the three kinds of data. This page asks whether network size can be estimated by counting geometric regions. K hyperplanes in general position cut d-dimensional space into at most M, the sum of C of K and m for m from 0 to d; the three lines are d equal to 1, 2, 3 with K from 1 to 4: for d equal to 2 they are 2, 4, 7, 11 and for d equal to 3 they are 2, 4, 8, 15. Example: d equal to 2 and K equal to 2 gives 1 plus 2 plus 1, which is 4. A hyperplane is a line in 2D and a plane in 3D, and the boundary of one hidden unit is one hyperplane. Bottom right is the real XOR construction: the two parallel lines of KP01 cut the plane into only three regions, not the general-position maximum of four. So the bound is only a ceiling, not a guarantee of quality. The next page asks which three strategies are used to choose a network size.

steps.label: Sizing strategies
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the geometric capacity bound is only a ceiling. This page asks which three strategies are used to choose a network size in practice. Analytic methods estimate capability by algebra or statistics and usually ignore the concrete optimisation. Pruning trains a larger network first and then deletes less important connections; it must be checked on validation data and the next KP covers it. Constructive methods grow from a small architecture, already seen in KP05, and must also be checked on validation data. The fourth column is the source's sine demo: target y equal to sin of 2 pi x plus noise, 15 training points and 10 test points, 3k plus 1 parameters; the source describes k of about 3 to 5 as suitable and k equal to 15 as possibly overfitting; this is not a universal optimum and this lecture did not rerun it. The main line ends here. The next page is an extension: two exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page covered the three sizing strategies. Two exercises to check. Exercise 1: training loss 0.40, 0.20, 0.10 and validation loss 0.45, 0.25, 0.30; which epoch? The hint is to find the validation minimum first. Exercise 2: how many regions at most do three lines in general position cut in two dimensions? The hint is to compute three binomial coefficients; is it still this number if the three are parallel? Try them yourself; the next page is the worked solution.

steps.label: Extension: worked solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page set two exercises. Exercise 1: among validation values 0.45, 0.25 and 0.30 the smallest is 0.25, so keep epoch 2; the lower training value of the last epoch does not change the choice, and epoch 3 validation is 0.05 above epoch 2. Exercise 2: C of 3 and 0 plus C of 3 and 1 plus C of 3 and 2 is 1 plus 3 plus 3, which is 7; three parallel lines give only four bands, short of the bound of seven. The geometric region count takes no part in picking a checkpoint. The next page is the last extension page: why the region count is a sum of binomial coefficients.

steps.label: Extension: recursion and code
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page worked out exercise 2 as 7 and three parallel lines as four bands. This page asks why the region count is a sum of binomial coefficients. Adding the K-th hyperplane in general position cuts some regions in two; the new parts correspond to the lower-dimensional regions the other K minus 1 hyperplanes form on it, so R of K and d equals R of K minus 1 and d plus R of K minus 1 and d minus 1, with R of 0 and d and R of K and 0 both equal to 1, and Pascal's relation gives the sum of binomial coefficients. Then the mean squared error: the loss is the average of the squared difference between target and output. The last line of code only picks an existing checkpoint and trains no network; real training must also save and restore that epoch's weights, fix the data split and record the metric. This is the last page of the unit; the next KP covers pruning.
